Keyframe spacing is the timing

One 1800 ms move, three key sets, straight-line in-betweens everywhere. Only where the keys sit changes — and that alone decides whether the move reads as mechanical, hand-drawn, or broken.

What to watch

  • Row A is not wrong, it is unargued. Nine keys, evenly spaced in value, evenly spaced in time, linear in-betweens: the dot crosses the rail at 0.56 track/s and never changes. Every in-between is correct and the move still reads as a machine, because nothing in the spacing says where it started or where it is going.
  • Row B moved nothing but the values. Same nine keys, same nine times, same total distance, same linear interpolation. Because the keys now bunch towards both ends of the rail, the speed goes 0.14 → 0.92 → 0.14 track/s: a 6.7× spread, and a 0 at both ends in the limit. This is slow-in / slow-out, and it is a statement about spacing, not about easing.
  • Slow-in / slow-out is not slower. It covers the same distance in the same 1800 ms, so it must be faster somewhere: its peak is 0.92 track/s against row A's constant 0.56 — 1.66× the average. Easing redistributes speed; it cannot create or destroy the average.
  • Row C is what three keys cost you. Keys at t = 0, 0.25, 1 force speeds of 1.11 and 0.37 track/s, so the dot hits a 3× corner at t = 0.25 and the eye reads a hitch. This is not a defect of linear interpolation: a three-stop @keyframes rule (or a three-point timeline in any editor) has exactly this shape, because keyframe percentages are times and the values in between are lerped.
Do not ease twice. An easing curve applied on top of eased spacing multiplies the two: cubic-bezier(.42,0,.58,1) over row B gives the middle ~6.7× speed spread of B and the 1.72× peak of the curve, and the start becomes static. If the keys already carry the timing, the curve should be linear; if the motion is one key pair, the curve has to carry everything.
